To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the DNA-dependent RNAP of Escherichiacoli binds a single-stranded RNA promoter loop, rather than double-stranded DNA, at its initiation site.

the E. coli DNA-dependent RNAP can bind and initiate transcription at an external loop of RNA, that this binding is similar to that observed for DNA templates, and that this binding is dependent upon the presence of both beta and beta' polymerase subunits.
the RNA promoter is recognized by the RNAP through binding of the beta and beta prime subunits, and that this binding is to a large single-stranded loop.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction between an RNA promoter and the E. coli RNA polymerase.
the molecular mechanism of promoter recognition by DNA-dependent RNA polymerases.
the interaction between the DNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RNAP) and RNA promoters and how this interaction can be used for the development of novel RNA vaccines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the RNA polymerase from Escherichica coli binds to a large external single stranded RNA loop, which is similar to the binding site for DNA promoters, but the binding site is located in a different position on the promoter.

the RNA promoter is bound by the beta' subunit of the RNAP in a similar manner as DNA promoters, however the binding site for the beta subunit is located at an external single-strand RNA loop rather than a double stranded RNA/DNA region.
the RNAP binds to the RNA promoter via the beta and beta'subunits, and that the binding site is a large single stranded RNA hairpin loop.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding site for the RNAP on a RNA promoter is a single-stranded loop that is bound by the beta and beta'subunits.
the DNA-dependent RNAP can recognize and initiate transcription from an RNA promoter in vitro.
the binding site for RNA polymerase to RNA promoters is similar to the binding site for DNA promoters.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the RNA polymerase binds to the RNA promoter in an analogous way to the way it binds DNA promoters, which is consistent with the fact that the RNA polymerases from bacteria are highly similar to their DNA polymerase counterparts.
DNA-dependent RNAP is capable of recognizing and initiating RNA transcription from RNA promoters.
the RNAP binds the RNA promoter at a site similar to that of a DNA promoter.
